evidence.claim: A river crossing leads to meadows shaped by centuries of farming.
evidence.quote: farmscapes of the Great Meadows in South Glastonbury that preserve 17th-century land use patterns

evidence.claim: Route 160’s scenic section runs 1.06 miles from the Connecticut River to Roaring Brook in Glastonbury.
evidence.quote: A 1.06-mile (1.71 km) section of Route 160 in Glastonbury, running from the Connecticut River to Roaring Brook, is designated a scenic road.

evidence.claim: At the river, the Rocky Hill–Glastonbury Ferry carries the highway across the water.
evidence.quote: The road crosses the Connecticut River on the Rocky Hill–Glastonbury Ferry.

evidence.claim: The surrounding historic district includes ferry landings, farms, and a landing village; its Great Meadows retain seventeenth-century land-use patterns.
evidence.quote: The historic district also encompasses farmscapes of the Great Meadows in South Glastonbury that preserve 17th-century land use patterns

evidence.claim: The surrounding historic district includes ferry landings, farms, and a landing village
evidence.quote: It includes the ferry landings and water traversed by the Rocky Hill – Glastonbury Ferry, one of the longest-running ferry services the nation, and the surrounding farmscapes and ferry landing village.

evidence.claim: The crossing began in 1655, when both banks belonged to Wethersfield.
evidence.quote: Started in 1655, it actually began before the foundation of the towns of Glastonbury and Rocky Hill, both towns being part of Wethersfield at that time.

evidence.claim: A poled raft gave way to horse power on a treadmill, then to steam in 1876.
evidence.quote: Originally a raft that was poled across the Connecticut River, it was then powered by a horse on a treadmill before being upgraded to a steamship in 1876.

evidence.claim: In 1932, the ferry became part of the newly commissioned Route 160.
evidence.quote: In 1932, it was incorporated into the newly commissioned Route 160.

evidence.claim: Glastonbury later sought an eastward extension to the New London Turnpike near Route 2, but the state declined the request in 1960.
evidence.quote: In 1960, a request by the Town of Glastonbury to extend Route 160 east to the New London Turnpike, near Route 2, was declined by the state.

evidence.claim: Traveling east from the ferry, the scenic section begins at the river and ends at Roaring Brook.
evidence.quote: A 1.06-mile (1.71 km) section of Route 160 in Glastonbury, running from the Connecticut River to Roaring Brook, is designated a scenic road.

evidence.claim: Near that eastern end, the John Hollister House stands on Tryon Street just west of the brook.
evidence.quote: The John Hollister House stands on the west side of the village of South Glastonbury, on the north side of Tryon Street (Connecticut Route 160) just west of Roaring Brook.

evidence.claim: The numbered highway continues to Route 17 in South Glastonbury.
evidence.quote: In Glastonbury, it continues east to end at an intersection with Route 17 in South Glastonbury.

evidence.claim: Three cars fit on the Hollister III, the ferry barge towed by the diesel-powered Cumberland.
evidence.quote: Today's ferry is a 3-car barge named the Hollister III towed by a diesel towboat named the Cumberland.

evidence.claim: That pairing follows a succession of ways to cross the Connecticut River: a poled raft, a horse working a treadmill, and a steamship introduced in 1876.
evidence.quote: Originally a raft that was poled across the Connecticut River, it was then powered by a horse on a treadmill before being upgraded to a steamship in 1876.

evidence.claim: The service began in 1655, before Rocky Hill and Glastonbury became separate towns.
evidence.quote: Started in 1655, it actually began before the foundation of the towns of Glastonbury and Rocky Hill, both towns being part of Wethersfield at that time.

evidence.claim: The ferry and its landings became part of a National Register historic district in 2005, following a proposal intended to help preserve the crossing.
evidence.quote: The ferry landings and the ferry itself are included in the Glastonbury–Rocky Hill Ferry Historic District, which was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2005. The National Register listing was proposed in 2005 to help preserve the historic ferry.

evidence.claim: The ferry crossing is seasonal.
evidence.quote: The Rocky Hill–Glastonbury Ferry is a seasonal ferry crossing

evidence.claim: The Great Meadows preserve seventeenth-century land-use patterns, with Colonial and Greek Revival farmhouses within the ferry historic district.
evidence.quote: farmscapes of the Great Meadows in South Glastonbury that preserve 17th-century land use patterns and Colonial and Greek Revival farmhouses

evidence.claim: Agriculture here predates English settlement: Native Americans cultivated the broad Connecticut River floodplain before Wethersfield residents surveyed and divided it in the 1640s.
evidence.quote: The broad meadows in the Connecticut River flood plain were used agriculturally by Native American prior to the arrival of English colonists, and were surveyed and subdivided by Wethersfield residents in the 1640s.

evidence.claim: Houses went up above the floodplain along what became Tryon Street.
evidence.quote: Houses were built just above the flood plain on what is now Tryon Street.

evidence.claim: Later development added farm buildings and ferry infrastructure, while landowners maintained family and business connections across the river.
evidence.quote: Later development in the 18th and 19th centuries added farm buildings and ferry-related infrastructure to the Glastonbury side of the district.  Landowners in this area retained and maintained family and business connections with those across the river.

evidence.claim: The John Hollister House has larger windows than it began with: its window openings were enlarged in the nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: The window bays are 19th-century enlargements of what were originally smaller openings

evidence.claim: Built about 1675 by John Hollister, Jr., it began as two rooms with a chimney.
evidence.quote: The house was built about 1675 by John Hollister, Jr.

evidence.claim: The central chimney remains part of a wood-frame house with a gabled roof and clapboard exterior.
evidence.quote: It is a 2+1⁄2-story wood-frame structure, with a gabled roof, central chimney, and clapboarded exterior.

evidence.claim: Its second floor projects slightly over the five-bay front, and the roof extends into a deep eave.
evidence.quote: Its front facade is five bays wide, with a center entrance and a slightly overhanging second floor.  The roof has a shallow pitch, and has a deeper than normal eave over a simple box cornice.

evidence.claim: The house stands on Tryon Street, just west of Roaring Brook.
evidence.quote: on the north side of Tryon Street (Connecticut Route 160) just west of Roaring Brook.

evidence.claim: it began as two rooms with a chimney
evidence.quote: The house was originally built as a two-room structure with chimney

evidence.claim: On the Glastonbury side, broad floodplain meadows meet houses set above the floodplain along Tryon Street.
evidence.quote: The broad meadows in the Connecticut River flood plain

evidence.claim: Across the water at Rocky Hill, a steep bluff separates the ferry landing from the town’s main economic center.
evidence.quote: A steep bluff separates the landing itself from the main town economic center

evidence.claim: houses set above the floodplain along Tryon Street
evidence.quote: Houses were built just above the flood plain on what is now Tryon Street.

evidence.claim: Roaring Brook’s grist and saw mills helped spur South Glastonbury’s development as the town’s first village.
evidence.quote: South Glastonbury developed as the town's first village, spurred in part by the development of grist and saw mills on Roaring Brook to the east.

evidence.claim: Rocky Hill’s landing became a port after a flood in 1700 destroyed Wethersfield’s old port, adding a shipping role to this riverbank.
evidence.quote: the Rocky Hill Landing area became its principal port area after a major flood in 1700 wiped out Wethersfield's old port area.

evidence.claim: In 1871, the Connecticut Valley Railroad reached the Rocky Hill landing area, providing another way to carry South Glastonbury’s goods to market.
evidence.quote: The Connecticut Valley Railroad was built through the landing area in 1871, providing transport to market for goods produced in South Glastonbury.

evidence.claim: It is Glastonbury’s oldest surviving colonial structure; John Hollister’s father’s house, credited as the town’s first, no longer stands.
evidence.quote: it is the town's oldest surviving colonial structure

evidence.claim: A two-story gabled extension reaches behind the house.
evidence.quote: A two-story gabled ell extends to the rear.

evidence.claim: John Hollister’s father’s house, credited as the town’s first, no longer stands
evidence.quote: whose father is credited with building Glastonbury's first house (which no longer stands).
